Der von nicht wenigen als Rassist bezeichnete Jordan Peele bekommt ein dickes Budget für sein Regie-Debüt, um in einem reinen Fantasy-Film die Realität zu verdrehen. Der Rest ist Filmgeschichte, leider derart Status. Vier „Nur-weil-ich-schwarz-bin“-Oscar-Nominierungen für eine allseits hofierte Hass-Tirade und einen Genre-Beitrag, wie er bis dahin bei derartigen Veranstaltungen gar nicht beachtet wurde. Die Frage nach dem Warum ist vermutlich einfach beantwortet, an einer herausragenden Qualität des Werkes liegt es sicher nicht: So viele Jahre indoktrinierter Komplex, meist schon seit der Wiege. Dieser Film ist das vielgesuchte feierliche Eingeständnis: Schuldig, schuldig, weiß zu sein. Wenn nicht Schuldeingeständnis, dann Schuldzuweisung. Zur Geschichte: Ein weißer junger Mann läuft abends mit seiner dunkelhäutigen Freundin durch Harlem. Nun ja, fast. Das hier ist kein Kurzfilm, er geht 105 Minuten. Sonst stört sich das vermeintlich bessere Publikum, genau das, welches hier nicht nur Unterhaltung sucht, sondern immer ein Statement findet, ja immer am billigen Kniff der Jump-Scares. Bei Peele sind jene als hochfrequentiertes Stilmittel ausnahmsweise erlaubt. Der Rest läuft auch nach Schema F: Einführung, Fragezeichen, erwarteter Plot-Twist, exzessives Ende. Dann doch eine stimmige Tour de Force, wenigstens ein einigermaßen genießbarer Genre-Happen? Wie man es nimmt: von unappetitlich („für das größere Ziel wird auch das Bett mit dem kleineren Ziel geteilt“) über unverschämt („alle Weißen wären insgeheim gern schwarz“) bis unerträglich („die weiße Bestie“). Da haben wir ihn, den „The Birth of a Nation“ unserer Zeit, allerdings einen „The Downfall of a Nation“. Nein zu Spaltung und derartigem Rassismus! ENGLISH Jordan Peele, described by quite a few as a racist, is given a hefty budget for his directorial debut to distort reality in a pure fantasy film. The rest is film history – unfortunately, that’s just the way it is. Four ‘just-because-I’m-black’ Oscar nominations for a universally fawned-over tirade of hatred and a contribution to the genre that had previously gone entirely unnoticed at such events. The question of why is probably easy to answer; it certainly isn’t down to the outstanding quality of the work: so many years of indoctrinated insecurity, mostly instilled from the cradle. This film is the much-sought-after solemn admission: guilty, guilty of being white. If not an admission of guilt, then an attribution of blame. The story goes like this: a young white man is walking through Harlem one evening with his dark-skinned girlfriend. Well, almost. This isn’t a short film; it runs for 105 minutes. Otherwise, the supposedly more discerning audience – precisely those who aren’t just looking for entertainment here, but always find a statement, and are always on the lookout for the cheap trick of jump scares – would take offence. With Peele, however, these are, for once, permitted as a frequently used stylistic device. The rest also follows a formulaic pattern: introduction, a question mark, the expected plot twist, an over-the-top ending. So is it a coherent tour de force after all, or at least a reasonably enjoyable slice of genre fare? It depends on how you look at it: ranging from distasteful (‘for the greater good, one shares the bed with the lesser good’) to outrageous (‘all white people would secretly like to be black’) to unbearable (‘the white beast’). There it is, the ‘The Birth of a Nation’ of our time – though in this case, ‘The Downfall of a Nation’. No to division and racism of this sort!

Honestly, this film wasn't very enjoyable to watch; it wasn't the kind of film I wanted to finish quickly, eager to see what would happen next. The flow was a bit lacking. While watching, especially the dialogues in the final scenes kept me engaged, otherwise it was very boring, or maybe my expectations were too high based on social media. I was thinking, "Why didn't I like this film, which is so popular?", but then I did some research and when I read the full version of the story, I understood the system the film was criticizing much better, and my interest in the film increased. The first aspect criticized in the film is: The Commodification and Exploitation of the Black Body: The Armitage family auction scene is a modern representation of the historical slave trade. Black people's genetics, physical strength, agility, or artistic talents (like Chris's photography skills) are admired by whites; however, this admiration stems not from respect, but from a desire to steal and possess those qualities. The dark and desperate void into which Chris is hypnotized represents the suppression of Black individuals' voices in society, their loss of control even over their own bodies, and their marginalization and passivization by the system. Micro-Attacks and Alienation: The questions Chris encounters at the garden party (genetic advantages, athletic ability, etc.) are examples of the racist stereotypes disguised as praise that Black people are subjected to in daily life. The film shows that racism is not just about hate speech; consuming a culture, body, or talent for one's own benefit and ignoring its true owner is one of the most dangerous dimensions of racism. Honestly, the sarcastic questions directed at Chris felt good, but they could have filmed it differently, making it both more enjoyable and engaging to watch, while also conveying the message effectively as it is. It's a good film, just a little boring.

Lots of stuff that works and lots of stuff that doesn’t. Nice social commentary, some really sharp symbolism, and creative metaphors. Some scenes use tension really well, along with some inspired cinematography. But the tonal mess that this movie is can sometimes be simply too much. None of the comedic scenes worked for me, not even a little bit. I would cut out the TSA guy entirely. I don’t believe comedic relief is really necessary in horror movies (especially when it lacks comedy), but most importantly, the job of comedic relief is to relieve tension. Why the hell would you want to relieve tension in a horror film? It seems as though Peele’s background in comedy is hindering his potential as a serious horror director. To clarify, I don’t think you can’t mix genres; I don’t believe in limitations in art. But here, the genre-breaking doesn’t seem to serve any purpose other than wasting my time. Aside from all that, the movie was also uneven in a plethora of ways: some scenes are brilliantly written and directed (helped a lot by some exceptional performances), while others are laughably cliché and interfere with the movie’s strengths. I think a great screenplay is hidden in here but is in dire need of a rewrite. As for Mr. Peele, I can see his obvious talent and potential, and I’m interested to see whether he manages to live up to it in his later projects, which I’m intending to watch.

Jordan Peele isn’t all misses at least. One thing that’s rarely weak in a Jordan Peele movie is the acting, and this movie is no exception. Allison Williams Absolutely kills it with the unsettling vibes and switch towards the end of the movie, outstanding work. Same goes for Daniel Kaluuya who bring easily my favorite performance of his career specially with his eyes truly disappearing into the terror and unforgettableness of the situation. Also like most Jordan Peele work it’s very well shot, very pleasant to look at in terms of quality and color and the score is perfection. The reason this movie hit for me though is cause the story was actually captivating and believable and the characters all take actions that make total sense. Chris isn’t just gonna sit there and be freaked out he actively is on alert the whole time even before visiting the house and he keeps a keen eye on everything, plus he fights his own way out of the situation in an extremely believable way without having to rely on any conveniences. Ro  being worried about him and finding a way to get to him also made total sense, and the cops not believing him yet him still pressing forward was great. Part of me did worry at the end that they were gonna pull a mega twist when Chris asked how he found him and reveal that Rob had the procedure or something but I’m glad they didn’t and just played it as a joke. The motivations also made total sense. These people are clearly racist but not in a way that is the overtly obvious kind that can get a bit much and can demean the core message, no they do view black people as superior in a way but more in the sense of jealousy and wanting what they have and viewing them simply as a vessel for themselves. Still inherently  very racist way of looking at things but done in a way at that I haven’t seen many stories tackle cause instead of the down your throat distracting kind, it more challenges the subtle ways we might think about or approach certain people in a way that clearly alienates them whether purposeful or accidental/negligent. Overall I was very pleased with this movie and now having completed the Peele trilogy I’m at least happy I liked one of them.
